source: Mirzaei (2026) Sample More, Reflect Less: Self-Refine and Reflexion lose to repeated sampling at equal token cost
finding: Re-runs the Wang et al. budget-matched comparison as a designed experiment. Methods where the model inspects its own output lose to plain repeated sampling at equal tokens. Reflexion as published never triggered a retry on the 1.5B model, so it became a cheap single chain of thought.
numbers: 7 methods, open 1.5B/3B/7B models, 2 math sets, 150 questions each, 36 paired comparisons, every token counted. After Holm correction 0 methods beat self-consistency, 10 are worse, 26 tied. All 18 comparisons involving self-inspection (Self-Refine, forced Reflexion, Best-of-N) are negative. Majority vote beats model-picked Best-of-N by 8.0 and 11.3 points at 1.5B, 2.0 and 1.3 at 7B (not distinguishable from zero). Self-Refine and forced Reflexion stay 3.6 to 10.1 points below the equal-cost baseline at 7B.
quote: Spending tokens to reconsider an answer is a worse use of them than spending the same tokens on another attempt
limits: Math with checkable answers only; models up to 7B; 8-bit weights; no frontier models; no external test signal, so it tests intrinsic reflection, not Reflexion with unit tests. Author says the curves may cross at frontier scale.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 4 for small models: a reflect-and-retry loop must be compared with plain resampling at equal tokens. Our scaffold should log tokens per arm and include a resample arm. Also log whether a self-triggered retry ever fires.

source: Verma (2026) Try Again, Don't Look Back: Blind resampling outperforms self-repair in small code models
finding: Placebo-controlled test of what in a failure-retry packet helps. Showing the model its own failed program makes it anchor on it. Execution feedback adds nothing measurable beyond a content-free 'wrong' notice. Retrieved solutions to OTHER tasks change nothing.
numbers: MBPP+, Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B/3B/7B, k=8 retries. Conditioning on own failed attempt costs 6.1 points at 1.5B (p=0.006); tied with best at 7B. Blind resampling uses 2.5x to 5.5x fewer tokens. Near-identical retry program in 33-68% of retries vs 2-14% under blind resampling. Reflection adds +0.8 points at 7B (not significant) for 2.5x output tokens. Retrieved cross-task experience within +-3.5 points. Penalty tracks baseline quality (r=0.96) across 6 configs, 2 model families. 46-53% of attainable gain is reached by retry 2.
quote: conditioning on the model's own failed attempt costs 6.1 points at 1.5B
limits: Small code models only; MBPP+; verbal reflection was self-generated. Does not test lessons stored across tasks and retrieved by trigger.
agent_relevance: Warning against showing the agent its own failed output when the lesson is meant to redirect. A lesson should state the trap and the alternative, not replay the failed attempt. Keep retries to about 2. Gives a concrete anchoring metric (similarity of consecutive attempts) to log.

source: Renze and Guven (2024) Self-Reflection in LLM Agents: Effects on Problem-Solving Performance
finding: Nine LLMs re-answered multiple-choice questions they got wrong, after eight kinds of self-reflection. All kinds beat baseline (p<0.001). More informative reflections (explanation, instructions, solution) beat thin ones (retry, keywords, advice). Even a bare 'you were wrong, try again' helped.
numbers: GPT-4 accuracy on previously wrong items: baseline 0.786, retry 0.827, keywords 0.832, advice 0.840, instructions 0.849, explanation 0.876, solution 0.925, composite 0.932, unredacted (answer leaked) 0.971. GPT-3.5: baseline 0.596, retry 0.686, explanation 0.802, solution 0.831. Llama 2 7B: 0.297, retry 0.372, explanation 0.457. Temperature 0, 10 exam sets.
limits: The model is told it was wrong (an oracle signal). Retry set is only items it failed, so the free signal inflates gains. Solution-type reflections leak answer structure. Not matched on tokens.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 1: richer failure explanations (cause plus how to solve) beat bare 'what went wrong'. But the oracle wrong-flag alone gave about half the gain for GPT-4, so any explanation arm must be compared against a content-free retry arm.

source: Anonymous authors (2026) VRL-Bench: benchmarking agents on computer control tasks under finite trial budgets
finding: Compares Reflexion and later verbal-memory methods against memory-free retry under a fixed trial budget. Each method beats retry in some settings and loses in others. Replaying reflections can lower success. A language-model scheduler that chooses between exploiting reflections and exploring (VEX2) is the only method positive over retry in all six settings.
numbers: Replay sweep: 3,324 recorded episodes; GPT-4o-mini actor, 134 ALFWorld and 100 HotPotQA cases. ALFWorld full replay 76.1% at trial 3 then plateaus; partial replay (alpha .25) reaches 81.3%; no replay 74.6%; AUC gain +7.1 points, selection-adjusted 95% CI [+0.9, +13.3]. HotPotQA full replay leads at trials 2-4 but ends 49% vs 50% no replay (diff -1.0, CI [-5.0, +3.0]). Full replay solves 15 ALFWorld cases no replay misses; no replay solves 13 that full replay misses. VEX2 vs retry at SR@6: +1.6 to +6.6 points MiniWoB, +8.0 to +17.0 WebShop; the two GLM-4.7-FlashX intervals include zero.
quote: each improves observed success over memory-free retry in some settings but reduces it in others
limits: One benchmark pair, small N, the authors propose VEX2 themselves; models include GPT-5.4 nano and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, not frontier.
agent_relevance: Resolves the Xing vs Reflexion conflict (K17) in part: reflection is a policy that sometimes hurts, so route between reuse and exploration. Supports a scaffold rule: after a lesson fails to help once, drop it and explore.

source: Wu et al. (2026) Towards Autonomous Memory Agents (U-Mem): learning-source ablation
finding: Ablation of learning source in a memory agent: success-only memory is weakest, failure-only contrastive memory is better, hybrid is best. Authors argue success memories reinforce what the model already knows, failure memories target blind spots.
numbers: HotpotQA, Qwen2.5-7B (mean +- std): success-only 50.80+-1.12, failure-only 51.60+-0.45, hybrid U-Mem 52.40+-0.89. Failure-only gain over success-only is 0.8 points, inside one std. Stronger models, Table 5: Gemini-2.5-flash AIME25 no memory 46.67, ReasoningBank 52.00, U-Mem 54.00; HotpotQA 62.40, 68.40, 71.60. DeepSeek-chat AIME25 46.67, 48.67, 50.67. Append-only store (no merge/delete) loses 3.2 points.
limits: Differences of 0.8 to 1.6 points are within noise. Table labels are garbled in extraction; mapping follows the prose. Single benchmark for the ablation.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence on gap 2: failure lessons add a little over success lessons, hybrid best. Keep both kinds in the store, do not drop recipes for warnings.

source: Wu et al. (2026) U-Mem retrieval-number sweep
finding: Number of retrieved memories K has an inverted U. Too many memories dilute the prompt.
numbers: HotpotQA, Qwen2.5-7B: K=1 50.20+-1.10, K=3 52.40+-0.89, K=5 50.80+-0.84, K=10 48.80+-0.84. Experience pool scaling 0 to 1000 tasks: 37.80 to 52.40 with no plateau under curation.
limits: One model, one dataset; U-Mem uses utility-aware Thompson sampling, so raw-similarity retrieval may degrade sooner. Granularity (raw case vs insight vs cluster) not swept here.
agent_relevance: Closes part of gap 6: K=3 beats K=1 and K=10 here; consistent with Memento K=4. Start with K=2 to 4 and sweep. Granularity still unswept.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs
finding: Consolidated lessons written by an LLM rewriting memory after each episode first help, then degrade, and can fall below no-memory. Even consolidating from ground-truth solutions, GPT-5.4 failed on 54% of ARC-AGI problems it had solved with no memory. Keeping raw episodes stays competitive; agents given Retain, Delete, Consolidate actions mostly retain raw episodes and double the accuracy of forced consolidation.
numbers: WebShop with AWM (50 held-out episodes): no-memory success 0.39; raw trajectories stay high while AWM-distilled memory falls as examples grow from 8 to 128 (Fig. 1b, values partly garbled). ScienceWorld with CLIN: utility rises then declines for memory sizes 16 and 50. ARC-AGI Stream: forced consolidation about half the accuracy of retain-by-default; episodic-only matches the auto regime.
quote: consolidated memories produced by today's LLMs are often faulty even when derived from useful experiences
limits: ARC-AGI and two agent benchmarks; authors' own study; not specific to failure lessons.
agent_relevance: Strong argument for gap 6: store raw failure episodes (task, wrong step, outcome) and derive the lesson at read time, or gate consolidation. Avoid rewriting the lesson store after every episode.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: experience-following behaviour
finding: Agents copy the output of the most similar stored input (experience following), so wrong records propagate (error propagation) and seemingly fine records can mislead (misaligned replay). Deletion rules compared: periodic, history-based (delete records whose later retrievals led to poor outcomes), and combined. With a strict evaluator, history-based deletion gave the best score; combined cut memory most.
numbers: Four agents (RegAgent synthetic, EHRAgent, AgentDriver, CIC-IoT). Coarse evaluator: periodic deletion gives large size cuts with small loss. With a strict evaluator, history-based deletion on AgentDriver exceeded an error-free-memory baseline. With a poor evaluator history-based deletion could hurt (GPT-4o-mini evaluator helped EHRAgent, hurt AgentDriver); fine-tuned evaluators were stable. Per-cell scores in Table 2 not mapped because of garbled extraction.
limits: Exact per-rule numbers not recovered; claims follow the prose. Synthetic and domain agents, not failure-lesson stores.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partly closed: a hybrid rule (periodic plus use-history deletion) is best supported, but needs a reliable utility signal. In our store record per lesson the retrieval count and the outcome after use; expire lessons whose use correlates with failure.

source: Wang et al. (2026) MemGuard: persisting verifier signals for LLM-agent memory governance (ablation)
finding: A separate failure-guard channel (negative records injected as avoid-cues, at most 2 alongside up to 5 positive records) gives a small but consistent gain; governance (dedupe, staleness, conflicts) matters much more.
numbers: Qwen-3.5-Plus success metric (Terminal-Bench 2.0 / SWE-Bench Verified / WebArena / Mind2Web): Full 67.4/83.6/58.4/51.8; without failure memories 66.1/82.2/56.5/50.7 (drops 1.3, 1.4, 1.9, 1.1); without admission 64.4/80.9/52.8/48.0; without governance 63.7/79.8/52.0/46.8; semantic-only retrieval 63.4/79.4/50.1/45.8. Removing failure guards mainly inflates average steps. Beats ReasoningBank in 16 of 16 backbone-benchmark cells, up to 7.9 points on WebArena. 5 seeds, matched budgets.
limits: Authors' own method and ablation; guards are bundled with a verifier so the isolated value of a warning versus a recipe is not measured.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 evidence: the warning channel is worth about 1 to 2 points, governance about 4 to 7. Priority for our schema: admission and expiry first, warning channel second. Cap warnings at 2 and keep them separate from positive recipes.

source: Wang et al. (2026) MemGuard verifier audit and noise stress test
finding: Measures how accurate the self-judged success label has to be. The verifier agrees with author inspection 86% (Qwen-3.5-Plus) and 83% (Flash). Post-hoc check against benchmark outcomes: 88.1% macro balanced accuracy, 9.3% false-positive rate. At 30% simulated label noise MemGuard loses 0.3 to 2.6 fewer points than a verifier-only filter.
numbers: Post-hoc join of 51,896 of 52,280 frozen task decisions. Governance blocks 38 of 60 false accepts before active-memory promotion. The verifier-only control beats ReasoningBank in 15 of 16 cells but loses to MemGuard in all 16.
limits: Noise is simulated label flips, not realistic confabulated lessons (Dixit). No sweep finds the break-even accuracy where memory falls below no-memory.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 only partly closed: at about 88% judge accuracy a governed store still wins and 30% label noise degrades but does not erase gains. The break-even point is still unmeasured. Keep lessons in a provisional state until a later outcome confirms them.

source: Anonymous authors (2026) ConMem: structured memory-guided adaptation in training-free multi-agent systems
finding: Signed cards: positive cards hold strategies, negative cards hold failure-derived avoid-cues. A negative card fires only if expected avoided loss exceeds false-suppression loss plus context cost. Removing failure reflection or failure admission each lowers accuracy.
numbers: Four ablations (no graph expansion, no coordination, no failure reflection, no failure admission) on KodCode and TriviaQA with AutoGen and CAMEL hosts. Largest drop is from removing coordination (-3.30 on CAMEL TriviaQA). Sizes of the failure ablations are only in bar charts. Gains up to 12.4 (AutoGen KodCode) and 11.5 (PDDL).
limits: Failure-ablation sizes not extractable; effect smaller than coordination. Not an isolated test of warning versus recipe.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: gives the formal firing rule p > (G + c)/(L + G) for a warning, which is the test needed to limit wrong firings. Implement as a relevance check with a counted false-fire rate.

source: Tsui (2026) Self-Correction Bench (v3, COLM 2026): reasoning-model results
finding: Reasoning models show a small or even negative self-correction blind spot, unlike non-reasoning models (64.5% average over 14 models). Appending 'Wait' to a non-reasoning model cuts the blind spot by 89.3% and moves it close to a reasoning model.
numbers: DeepSeek-V3-0324 0.567 to 0.902 with Wait vs DeepSeek-R1-0528 0.908. Claude 3.5 Haiku blind spot 52.5%, Sonnet 4 41.4%. 62.8% average blind spot in logic and object-tracking tasks. Most common first word after an error for R1-0528 is 'No' (0.324) or 'But'.
limits: Synthetic injected errors, not natural ones. Blind spot is about locating a planted error, not final-answer gain on natural tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: a forced 'Wait' re-check is a cheap trigger for non-reasoning models. For reasoning models it is largely built in, so an extra scaffold re-check buys little (see d13).

source: Zhang et al. (2025) CorrectBench: can LLMs correct themselves?
finding: Self-correction helps on complex reasoning; mixing strategies helps further but costs efficiency. For reasoning LLMs, added self-correction gives only marginal gains at high time cost, and a simple chain-of-thought baseline is competitive.
numbers: Three tasks (commonsense, math, code); instruction models vs reasoning models. Reasoning models showed slight gains on some sets (CSQA, GPQA, MATH) and marginal declines on others. Per-dataset numbers not extracted.
limits: Some correction methods use ground-truth or external signals; no equal-token comparison.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 answer: the 2023 negative result is largely superseded for reasoning models, and extra reflection loops on top of them have marginal value. Spend tokens on resampling or external checks.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A critical survey
finding: No major prior work shows successful intrinsic self-correction under fair settings in general tasks. Many positive results used oracle info or weak initial prompts. Self-correction works with reliable external feedback or on decomposable tasks (e.g. CoVe verifying each listed item).
numbers: Table 4 flags RCI (ground-truth answers, only revises wrong ones), Reflexion on HotpotQA (exact match to ground truth as feedback), CAI revisions and Self-Refine (weak initial prompts) as unrealistic or unfair.
quote: no major work shows successful self-correction of responses from LLMs using feedback generated by prompting themselves under fair settings
limits: Survey up to mid-2024; before reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Supports splitting failures by whether a reliable external signal exists (gap 5): if yes, reflect and retry; if no, resample or verify per item. Our verify state should say which signal it relies on.

source: Cheng et al. (2026) TAME and Trust-Memevo: memory misevolution
finding: Even in benign task streams, score-driven memory evolution erodes trustworthiness (safety, privacy, fairness). A trust-aware executor/evaluator loop that grades each used memory limits this.
numbers: Abstract level: on GPT-5.2 AIME the framework improves accuracy by 14.6 points; naive evolution shows decline in trustworthiness across tasks.
limits: Only abstract and introduction read; numbers beyond the abstract not checked; safety focus rather than accuracy.
agent_relevance: Adds a second failure axis for lesson stores: they can raise score while lowering safety. Include a safety check on stored lessons.

source: Zhu et al. (2025) Where LLM agents fail and how they can learn from failures (AgentErrorTaxonomy, AgentDebug)
finding: Taxonomy of failure modes in memory, reflection, planning, action and system modules, with root-cause isolation and corrective feedback. Abstract and results table re-checked.
numbers: AgentErrorBench all-correct accuracy 24.3% vs 0.3% for direct prompting, step accuracy 45.0% vs 28.0%; up to 26% relative task-success gain on ALFWorld, GAIA, WebShop. Brute-force and binary-search baselines score 0.0 to 0.3% all-correct.
limits: Annotated rollouts; recovery gain relies on a strong root-cause finder (small models performed poorly).
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a failure-type label (plan, action, memory, reflection) is needed before choosing a repair. Type the failure first, then write the lesson.

source: Understanding the weakness of LLM agents within a complex Android environment (AndroidArena)
finding: Seen only in a search result: authors report Reflexion did not beat plain re-execution of failed tasks in cross-app Android tasks.
limits: Snippet only; not opened. Likely the Xing et al. result already counted in K17.
agent_relevance: Consistent with d02 and d04: informed retry is not reliably better than blind retry.

source: Hatalis et al. (2025) Review of case-based reasoning for LLM agents; ICCBR 2025 CBR-LLM workshop
finding: Searched for any independent modern CBR test of CHEF-style failure-indexed retrieval (gap 10). ICCBR 2025 and its CBR-LLM workshop list CBR for RAG, legal QA, LLM similarity assessment, and a note that giving LLMs cases can produce hallucinated explanations from those cases. No paper found that measures failure-indexed retrieval.
limits: Only search snippets; Springer table of contents and CEUR papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open: the CHEF mechanism has no direct modern replication; nearest tests are ConMem (negative cards) and MemGuard (failure guards).
